Peri Tzadik, Toldot 1: Read: the same two Tanchuma passages (joy at Isaac's birth; the angels' objection) and the same Rosh Hashanah 16b difficulty, with a different answer. Note at [2.9].
Akeidah as Abraham's water included in fire, explained as self-nullification; note at [4.59].
Same Tanna DeBei Eliyahu line used for love and fear completing each other; note at [4.63].
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 2: Explains Yitzchak's love for Esav from Onkelos, BR 63:10 and RSBG: the good in Esav overcame through kibbud av.
Same question on mat'amim, answered with joy for ruach hakodesh (Elisha's musician) and BR 65:13 sight/taste; Esav's kibbud av.
Yitzchak gave Esav kibbud-av mitzvos to merit; Rivkah's 'obey my voice' to add Yaakov's merit through his mother's command.
Asks the same 'כאשר אהבתי' question; answers through sparks and gevurah.
Menorat HaMaor, ix; On the Honoring of Parents, The ways of honoring
Esav inherited this world for feeding his father the game; feeding a parent brings blessing (Gen 27:25).
Reads BR 11:4 (Antoninus): on Shabbat the serpent's poison has less hold, so the taste itself changes.
On 'ברכו במטעמים': delighting the body on Shabbat is a mitzvah so the soul can rejoice in devekut.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 3: 'תברכך נפשי' = the Shechinah, which Rivkah rendered 'לפני ה''; Rav Tzadok links the same two verses (1.58, 1.65–66).
Read as Ketem Paz on Zohar 142a:3 (the ref given would not open): the kids as Pesach and Chagigah; Isaac tasted both; 'tasting' spiritual vs 'eating' physical.
Reads 'אם לקרבנך... למאכלך' as Yaakov knowing Yitzchak ate in holiness; table like an altar a fortiori; Rivkah understood 'לפני ה''.
Treats the Zohar as a dispute (Pesach/Chagigah vs Yom Kippur goats) and explains 'ומתרווייהו טעים' by Isaac's holiness, as Rav Tzadok does.
Explains Zohar II 61b: the spiritual flow inside physical food reaches each person by the level of his soul; close to 'מוצא פי ה' שבמאכל'.
The food a holy man eats is raised up as if offered on the altar; brings Ketubot 105b and Yoma 71a.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 4: Notes by Rabbi Yehoshua Hartman on Derashat Shabbat HaGadol 31:8-13
פירושים והערות מהרב יהושע הרטמן על דרשת שבת הגדול
Quotes Maharal (Ner Mitzvah): three kingdoms' hidden purity sign vs Edom's outward hooves, the same inner/outer contrast.
Leviathan feast = hidden light; cites Midrash HaNe'elam 135b and BB 75a.
Leviathan = subdued appetite reserved for the righteous; four impure animals = kingdoms. (Model ref 72 was wrong; 60 is the one that matches.)
"You hurried" and "Hashem made it happen" read as holiness in food drawn down without prayer.
Asks the same question on the kal va-chomer (why would food outrank an offering) with a different answer.
Isaac's meal includes wine as his attribute: "chamra de-mintra".
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 5: Opened: joins Bereshit Rabbah 65:22 (Yosef Meshita) with Sanhedrin 37a 'bogedav' as the os does, and explains the betrayers as the 'garment' of Jacob.
Jacob told the truth in 'אנכי עשו בכורך'; 'your firstborn' tied to 'העבודה בבכורים', the same move as 2.40.
Same question (how could Jacob, the attribute of truth, say something false), answered through 'Anochi' as the whole Torah.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 6: Ref as given returns 404; the passage with דרוכב/בעקימו/תתפל is Ohr HaChammah on Zohar 1:138a:6 (R. Chaim Vital): Jacob, a 'tam', goes crookedly with the serpent per עם עקש תתפל to keep it from holiness, which is the os's core idea.
Jacob outwitted Esau by 'ועם עקש תתפל' and received the blessings from both sides, the same verse and setting.
Degel Machaneh Ephraim, Addenda on Torah, Toldot 3
Asks how Jacob, a man of truth, said 'אנכי עשו'; answers via Onkelos בחכמה and BR 'בחכמת תורתו': Jacob is Torah.
Commentary on Rav Tzadok's Zohar I 145b: 'שכנתי ערמה דא יעקב', shrewdness as Jacob's left-side component that won the blessings.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 7: Reads each of the blessings (dew/earth = Z"A/Nukva, grain and wine = mochin, 'הוה גביר' = Esau's path as a servant's aid) as stages of the final tikkun; close to 1.37–1.44 and 3.10.
Elohim = judgment, so Jacob's blessings are conditional and Esau's not (Rashi's point at 1.21); סמכתיו as supports for a greater good.
Esau's this-worldly blessing was meant so he would prepare Jacob's bread and be rectified through him; 'ודגן ותירוש סמכתיו' as the core reserved for Jacob.
Dew = Keter, grain = Chokhmah 'called bread', wine = Binah: exactly Rav Tzadok's 2.4–2.17 mapping; also the seventy princes and Jacob 'above, above'.
Enumerates the same ten blessings item by item and ties them to other tens.
Develops the same Ra'aya Mehemna (III 124b) on scholars who resemble Shabbos and are sustained by weekday food, from the side of the tree of life.
Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Vayetzei, Torah Ohr 28
Explains the Tikkunim's 'Jacob outside, Moses inside' as Tiferes revealed vs its hidden Da'as, the basis of 3.14–3.17.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 8: Notes by Rabbi Yehoshua Hartman on Be'er HaGolah, Well 6 15:81-86
פירושים והערות מהרב יהושע הרטמן על באר הגולה
Quotes the same Sifrei (study Aggadah to know God and cleave to Him) with 'draws the heart'; supports [2.65]-[2.71] only, not the os's food theme.
Isaac's blessing of dew is the dew from Atika Kadisha, which matches 'the dew of Atika' at [3.29]; the matching word itself (שברכתו) is incidental.
Same argument: מוצא פי ה' in the bread; Rav Nachman's beef and the infant tasting grain prove that food adds wisdom; eating for Heaven strengthens Torah and prayer.
Shem MiShmuel, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah 3:8
Arizal on Deut 8:3: bread nourishes in proportion to the מוצא פי ה' within it, the 'well-known' reading of [1.15]-[1.16].
Isaac's blessing as Mikra and Mishnah drawing a light beyond measure (ארוכה מארץ מדה), passed to Jacob through Isaac's gevurah.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 10: It is the very passage Rav Tzadok cites (Zohar I 142a, R. Elazar on Psalms 84:6). Used as the source note, not as a separate parallel.
Reconciles Berakhot 17a with Pesachim 50b through Eruvin 13b's 'now that he was created', as Rav Tzadok does.
Same close reading, from the Chiddushei HaRim.
Peri Tzadik, Toldot 9: Links Isaac's 'I do not know the day of my death' to 'repent one day before your death' (Shabbat 153a), applied to Esau's teshuvah.
